lesson.title: Events: Naming Which Outcomes You Care About
lesson.summary: An event is a collection of outcomes from a random phenomenon grouped by some shared trait; this section shows how events let you ask focused questions about randomness.
lesson.body:
You already know that a random phenomenon has individual outcomes that can't be predicted with certainty one at a time, even though the process itself is well-defined. Once you have all those possible outcomes in mind, you almost never care about just one of them in isolation ,  you care about a whole group that shares something in common. That group is called an event. Formally, an event is any subset of the possible outcomes of a random phenomenon, and it's usually described not by listing every outcome but by stating a condition that outcomes must satisfy to belong to it.

Think about rolling two ordinary six-sided dice and adding the numbers that come up. The random phenomenon here is the pair of rolls; the full set of possible outcomes includes every combination like (1,1), (1,2), (2,1), all the way up to (6,6) ,  thirty-six equally likely pairs in total. Now suppose you're interested in "the sum is 7." That phrase describes an event, and it doesn't correspond to a single outcome but to a whole cluster of them: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), and (6,1). Six different outcomes, all lumped together because they share the property that their numbers add to 7. Notice that the event itself is just a description or a set ,  it's the condition "sum equals 7" that does the sorting, pulling six specific pairs out of the thirty-six possible ones.

Why bother separating outcomes from events at all? Because almost every real question you'll ask about randomness is phrased at the event level, not the outcome level. Nobody genuinely wants to know the chance of rolling exactly (2,5) as opposed to (5,2) ,  those are different outcomes but express the same practical idea, "one die shows 2, the other shows 5." What people actually want to know is things like "how likely is it that the sum is at least 10" or "how likely is it that both dice match." Each of those is an event, built by filtering the full outcome list down to the ones that fit a rule. Once you can name an event precisely, you can start counting how many outcomes belong to it, which is the first real step toward assigning it a probability later on.

It's worth noticing that events can be as narrow or as broad as you like, and the same set of outcomes can be described by more than one condition. "The sum is 7" and "the two numbers differ by an odd amount and add to 7" happen to pick out the same six outcomes here, since any pair summing to 7 automatically has one odd and one even number. An event can also contain just a single outcome ,  "you roll (3,3)" is a perfectly legitimate event with only one member ,  or it can contain nothing at all, like "the sum is 13," which is impossible with two six-sided dice and corresponds to an empty set of outcomes.

As you move forward, get comfortable translating everyday questions into event language before doing any counting or calculating. Ask yourself: out of every possible outcome of this random phenomenon, which ones actually satisfy the condition I'm interested in? Answering that question precisely ,  listing or characterizing exactly the outcomes that qualify ,  is what defines the event, and it's the groundwork every later idea about chance will be built on top of.
